query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an Al-rich surface alloy via pack cementation onto as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a stable alumina scale during high-temperature exposure in air, blocking oxygen ingress and preventing embrittlement without degrading the alloy’s tensile ductility or high-temperature yield strength relative to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.intervention: Introduce an Al-enriched surface layer using a pack cementation process, followed by a suitable heat treatment to grow an external alumina scale.
generation.conditions: Service at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours in air under tensile strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent alumina surface layer that impedes oxygen diffusion into the alloy substrate.
generation.mechanism: The Al-rich coating oxidizes preferentially, forming a protective alumina scale that lowers oxygen permeability and reduces interstitial embrittlement, thereby preserving strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant reduction in oxygen pickup at elevated temperature, retention or slight improvement of the baseline tensile ductility (≥8%) and yield strength (~≥160 MPa) at 1000 °C compared to uncoated samples.
generation.baseline: Uncoated cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxidation resistance and embrittlement at high temperatures, limiting ductility below useful levels over extended exposures in air.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies at 1000 °C in air for moderate strain rates (10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)). Ensuring scale adherence at longer exposures and higher temperatures may require additional verification.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term scale stability in thermal cycling, potential spallation during mechanical loading, and the influence of variations in pack cementation parameters remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture cast HfNbTaTiZr test coupons; apply an Al-rich pack cementation coating to half the coupons, with uncoated specimens as a baseline. Expose both sets in air for 100 h at 1000 °C under identical tensile loading. Compare post-exposure oxygen concentrations, surface scale microstructures, and remaining tensile properties of coated and uncoated samples.
measurements: Depth-resolved oxygen content (by EDS or SIMS)
Surface morphology and composition of oxide scale (by SEM/EDX)
Room- and high-temperature tensile properties of exposed vs. unexposed samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oxygen ingress is not reduced or mechanical performance does not surpass uncoated samples after testing, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
